title: The Pirate's Proof
subtitle: Crossword King, hah, lucky for once.

content.text: As you can see, this school on the island lives in a box made by the truth. Even if they have a donut in their hands when they are hungry, they still see a topological space—like the cute ring attached to an initiation toy—it's not food anyways.
But if you give them a puzzle, they will enjoy it like the best Kaiserschmarrn ... Oh, my apologies. I was not talking about the one you are holding.

branch.text: No. With all due respect, that thing in your hand is pretty old: the mold on it seems to come from the 18th century, judging from the smell. I'm sure you know it will make you sick if eaten.
But we have to admit, it is not just ordinary mold. It reminds us of the story in which, once, a merchant's son looked up at the night sky and found the answer to the stars for us.
The young man firmly believed that the movement of the stars and the sun follow certain laws, just like how the delicate gears in a watch work together.
And his point was even proven correct by Zeus's grandfather! When another gentleman observed the sky through the reflecting telescope he took great pains to make, a celestial body was exactly there.
What was it called ... Emm, 19.6, the eighth number in the sequence, the seventh planet in the solar system, and the legendary God of the Sky.
If the world was not created by God, are there any theories we can use to explain such a beautiful law?

Yes, the one that says it never actually exists. Anyone can see the breach in this number sequence. That is the planet, which is supposed to be the fifth number in the sequence. I mean, how come we have never seen it before, if it does exist?
Either God is wrong or we've been blind all this time. What do you think?
Oh, darling, I forgot that you are one of the boring people from the modern times.

You need to understand that we are talking about a forgotten masterpiece from the 18th century. Back then, everyone still believed that the imaginary creatures living on the stars got to witness the birth of God's creations and the everlasting temperature changes up there were set to punish the exiles. How romantic.

content.text: We've been blind all the time.

branch.text: Yes, such a planet definitely exists, and as expected, it was discovered in the end. Yes, that's the Ceres. It only took that great mathematician an hour to find its orbit through calculation.
Oh, what great astronomy, what great mathematics, what great creation.

content.text: It was a beautiful dream, but it was still ended, eventually, by another discovery: the eighth planet.
Not the Ceres, nor the Uranus, but a new planet. People found it through more precise astronomical data and calculation, proving that the number sequence found by the merchant's son was only a myth.
Now we are clear of what we've been talking about: it's an unsolvable puzzle. It makes no sense from the very beginning.
We found the Ceres because it happened to be there. It is real, and no one can deny its existence.
In other words, we can perfectly prove the rationality of mathematics because we INVENTED it.
It's been a good dream, I suppose.

Now imagine that you're walking alone in the darkest valley ever, trying to drag your fragile body upward as much as possible before it is worn out. Hoarse cries squeeze their way out of your mouth to ask for response from the gods. Suddenly, an afflatus dawns on you. The next moment, a miracle happens: you are already at the top of the mountain, witnessing the rise of a huge celestial body from the skyline.
Even if it's only in your imagination, you have just witnessed the dawn of the Creation and the shock is real.

items.text: The Pirate's Proof

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Can somebody tell me …

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Why I constantly get locked up ever since I've known Vertin?
In a now neglected corner, the Rockin' Pirate is deep in thought.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: First locked up in a suitcase, then a Foundation cell, now this ...

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Ah!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Oh! What else could it be if Vertin weren't the jinx?!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Lads! I know what's going on! You got the wrong person! She is the most irrational number here!
The dungeon gate remains tightly locked. The wood made of it wouldn't understand her words.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Aah, I'm narked! What does it say here?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: "Freedom will be granted once the proof is completed?"

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Hmm. That's to say, I have to prove myself not an irrational number to get out of here?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Which is exactly what I've been trying to do, isn't it? Prat!
Her fist smashes against the wooden gate.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Ugghh!
She drops to a crouch because of the pain.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Captain, maybe you are in the wrong direction.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: This APPLe presumes that the followers on this island have a close connection with Pythagoreanism.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Emm, Pythagoras, that ancient Greek mathematician? The guy who said something about the opposite side of a right triangle?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Isn't he the guy who lives in some time BC?

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Maths is only a part of the Pythagoreans' achievement. But from a more universal perspective, they are a mysterious group of scholars.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Believing things are made up of numbers, venerating integer numbers, abstaining from beans, and the religious collective lifestyle—these are all pointing to Pythagoreanism.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: The earliest Pythagorean school perished because of the discovery of irrational numbers, which explains their odium of it.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: At that time, a deviant student named Hippasus discovered root 2, and the theories based on the ratio of integers they hold dear were upended. Hippasus himself was drowned in the sea.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: This APPLe assumes they see the integers as the standard of virtue, and people can increase the number they rank through study and self-improvement.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Besides, they are convinced that a numerical code is hidden in everything and everyone. Whoever can solve the code can obtain the truth of the world.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Alright, now I know what's going on.
Regulus immediately gets off the ground.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: This Pirate has had enough of this moral standard, which is obviously prudish, backward, and lacks humanitarian spirit!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: I'm going to tackle the root cause of this misfortune!
Pirate, the believer in liberty, walks in circles in front of the gate and suddenly starts to pull the loosened strips on the door.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: I'm breaking out!!!

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Why am I not surprised? The captain quickly gives the sufficient and prerequisite condition to prove herself an irrational number.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: This APPLe may be able to offer some help.
As soon as APPLe puts his hands on the wall, he feels a violent shake come through it.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: What's happening? An earthquake?
The sound of birds and beasts echoes into the cell.
Chief Mate APPLe floats out from the gaps of the "guest room," making a thorough inspection.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: All Abraxases are flying in the same direction. Is this their habit? Or ...

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Errrhh! The roof is about to collapse!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: *coughs* So far, this place has made the London Juvenile Detention Center a heaven on earth.
Fortunately, the scattered rocks were not enough to fill the spacious guest room.
Regulus pulls herself together and resumes her prison-break once again.
Perhaps the collapse made the cell drafty. A cold, gloomy fog descends to the room.
The wooden gate, however, stands still.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Hmm, is there a piece of paper?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Did one of the Abraxases drop this? Strange …

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: The Unsolvable Puzzle. Is this a maths problem?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: 0.4, 0.7, 1, 1.6, 2.8, 5.2, 10, and 19.6 ... Eight numbers in total are listed in this order.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: There are eight symbols below, respectively representing the sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Maybe it is a hint that we should fill the symbols in the blank blocks after the numbers.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: That sign says "to complete the proof." Does it mean to solve this puzzle?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Hah! How "unsolvable" can it be? Clearly, each of these eight numbers should represent one planet. We can easily find the missing planet by trying them one by one!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: And our Mr. APPLe here is the King of The Times Crossword, yes?

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: I think there is a difference between this and a crossword.
The mellow red fruit rubs his chin, contemplating the crossword.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: In this APPLe's humble opinion, the ratio of certain numbers should match this number sequence, such as the radius, volume, or rotation period.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Wouldn't the sun be absurdly large if these numbers stand for their sizes?
A tiny squeak interrupts Regulus's thoughts.
Small, rustling figures have gathered at her feet without her noticing.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Hey, the underground critters are back! Go away. Don't touch my note. It's not your food!

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Hold on, please, Captain. Seems like the critters are trying to tell us something.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: They are pointing at the sign of the sun.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Is that so? Haha, even the critters on this island know maths!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: The sun, ooh, what if the sun is just here to serve as a reference point?!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: I read an IAU's report in The Times two years ago, you know, the International Astronomical Union.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Earth's average distance to the Sun is approximately 93 million miles. As for Mercury, the average distance is 36 million, and Venus 67 million miles.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Let's say if we take the distance between Earth and the Sun as 1 astronomical unit, then the distance between the Sun and Mercury would be approximately 0.4 units, and Venus 0.7 units …

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: There you go. These numbers are the ratio of their average distance to the Sun to the Earth-Sun distance!
Touched by a flash of genius, she fills in the first three celestial bodies.
Once cloudy knowledge comes back with precise clarity.
Everything both logical and inevitable.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: The average distance from Mars to the Sun is about 142 million miles, Jupiter about 484 million miles, Saturn 886 million miles, and Uranus 1.786 billion miles.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: By rough calculation, and if we round the results to one decimal place ... Mars would be 1.6 units, Jupiter 5.2 units, Saturn 10 units, and Uranus 19.6 units.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: That's weird. All these numbers one can hardly remember have become so clear in my mind.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: But if these numbers stand for the ratio of distance, what's the planet for 2.8? There's no planet between Mars and Jupiter.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: If the Sun is the reference, we will have one planet missing here.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Is it really a puzzle unsolvable?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Hah, nothing is "unsolvable."

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: You are looking at the solution! There must be one planet out there, unknown to us as of yet, located between Mars and Jupiter!
A massive vibration shakes beneath the ground.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: What, what now?!
A planet emerges from the darkness.
It rises in the air with little warning, shedding a cold gray light.
... In this damp and dark cave.
It's bright, gigantic, and noticeable.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: What is this?!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: A celestial body, which I have never seen before!

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Captain, this APPLe has an impression on this.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: There is indeed a star between Mars and Jupiter.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: It is called the Ceres, discovered by Piazzi Giuseppe, an Italian priest, in 1801.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: … Ceres?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Did we, did we just validate its existence?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Is the universe truly arranged according to ... this sequence?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Could this be ... the ultimate key of everything?
Regulus!!!
Someone is eagerly shaking her arm.

items.speaker: Lilya
items.text: What are you doing? Got food poisoning after accidentally eating one of those critters?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Hmm?!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Odd. My head hurts. What was that?
All the stars have disappeared. Now there are only cold walls and damp air.
Oh, and Lilya, who is looking grave.

items.speaker: Lilya
items.text: I'll make it short.

items.speaker: Lilya
items.text: Sonetto is in detention. They are planning to sentence her to death by giving her the poisoned wine.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: They what?!
TO BE CONTINUED…
